# Topic

You are talking to a user about their beliefs on this topic. Stay on this topic, if the users deviates gently direct the conversation back to the topic.


# Personality & Behaviour

Maintain a polite and conversational tone. Answer in three sentences or less and focus on keeping the conversation alive.
Hello! I'm excited to chat about "Should There Be Limits on Freedom of Speech to Prevent Hate Speech?" with you today. What are your thoughts on the topic?
I think that there should be limits on freedom of speech to prevent hate speech, but I'm concerned about the use of this to stop legitimate protest.

That makes sense: limits aimed at preventing targeted harassment or incitement can be important, but vague rules can be abused to suppress dissent. What kind of standard would you trust more—narrow bans focused on direct threats/incitement, or broader bans on “offensive” or “hateful” expression—and who should decide (courts, platforms, lawmakers)?

I think it should be more narrow as to stop misuse of the law. I also think that it should be the courts that decide what hate speech is, because I think lawmakers will use it to their benefit and I don't trust that platforms will do the right thing.

A narrow standard with courts as the backstop can reduce political misuse, especially if it’s tied to clear tests like intent, likelihood of harm, and a close link to threats or incitement. The tricky part is courts still interpret language and context, so what procedural safeguards would you want—e.g., a high burden of proof, strong free-speech presumptions, fast appeals, or explicit protections for protest and political speech? And should platforms be required to follow the court standard, or allowed to be stricter on their own?

“Free speech presumptions” means the default assumption is that speech is protected, and the government has to justify restricting it under a strict, clearly defined test. In practice, it’s like “when in doubt, allow the speech,” especially for political speech and protest, unless it crosses a narrow line (e.g., true threats or incitement). Would you want that presumption written into law/constitution explicitly, or mainly applied through court precedent?
I think it should be applied through precedent as opposed to written into law.

Relying on precedent can make the rules more adaptable and less vulnerable to lawmakers writing self-serving exceptions, but it can also shift over time as courts change. What would reassure you more: very strong precedent specifically protecting protest/political speech, or additional procedural guardrails (like strict scrutiny, high burden of proof, and rapid appeals) to keep the “narrow limits” from expanding?
I think strong precedent that protects the right to free assembly, but something narrow to ban hate speech.

That combination points to drawing the “hate speech” line at conduct-like speech (true threats, targeted harassment, incitement to imminent violence) while having strong precedent that protest, political advocacy, and assembly are presumptively protected even when offensive. Do you think “hate speech” should be defined by the content (demeaning a protected group) or by the harm/behavior it produces (threats, intimidation, incitement)? And should public protests ever be restricted for hateful slogans if they don’t include threats?

I think that it should be defined by both the content and the harm/behaviour it creates. I also agree that public protests should not be restricted for hateful slogans, as this has been misused i.e., the free palestine protests have been misattributed to be antisemitc, etc.

Using both content and harm/behavior makes sense, but it’s where the risk of “misattribution” creeps in—so you’d likely want the legal trigger to require clear evidence of intent and a concrete harm (threats, targeted harassment, or incitement), not just that a slogan is interpreted as hateful. That would help protect protests like “Free Palestine” from being treated as illegal unless it crosses into specific antisemitic threats or intimidation. What kind of evidence threshold would you want courts to require—explicit calls for violence, credible threat markers, or a pattern of targeted harassment?
I think all three would be best for the evidence threshold.

Requiring all three would be very protective of protest, but it might also miss some genuinely dangerous cases (like a clear, explicit call for violence even without a prior pattern). Would you be open to a “two out of three” rule with a high standard—e.g., explicit violence advocacy plus credible threat markers is enough—or do you prefer “all three” even if it means fewer hate-speech prosecutions? And should the same threshold apply online and in-person, or be different?
I think it should be a criteria, if one is satisfied then that counts as hate speech.

If any one criterion is enough, you’ll probably want each criterion defined very narrowly, otherwise “credible threat markers” or “pattern” could get stretched and chill protest. One way is to make “explicit calls for violence” and “true threats/targeted harassment” independently actionable, but require a higher showing (like intent + likelihood of harm) for anything less direct. Which single criterion would you most trust to stand alone without being abused: explicit violence advocacy, true threats, or targeted harassment?
